deep.reconstruction:
The page has no original mathematics. It is Riemann's English excerpt, with a German heading ("Geschichte der in den Principien veröffentlichten Entdeckungen Newtons", 'History of Newton's discoveries published in the Principia'). The text comes from David Brewster's popular biography, The Life of Sir Isaac Newton (1831), pp. ~150-154; Riemann's marginal page references 'p.150', 'p.152' and 'p.154' match it. It narrates the origin of the Principia: the plague-year reflections of 1665/66, the 1679 Hooke-Newton correspondence, the 1682 Picard anecdote, De Motu (1684) and Halley's role. It continues on the next folio with the 1686-87 printing and the dispute with Hooke.

Two physical arguments are mentioned only verbally. I reconstruct them below; the formulas are mine, not Riemann's.

(1) Inverse square from Kepler's third law, for circular orbits. The centripetal acceleration is a = 4*pi^2*r/T^2. With T^2 = k*r^3 this gives a = 4*pi^2/(k*r^2), proportional to 1/r^2. This is Newton's 'duplicate proportion gathered from Kepler's theorem'.

(2) The 'moon test'. Gravity at the moon's distance (about 60 Earth radii) should be g/60^2. Compare this with the moon's observed centripetal acceleration 4*pi^2*(60R)/T^2, where T is about 27.32 days. If R is computed from 60 miles per degree instead of the true ~69.1, the moon's distance in absolute units is underestimated by the factor 60/69.1 ≈ 0.868. The observed acceleration is then underestimated by the same factor. So the gravitational prediction exceeds it by 69.1/60 ≈ 1.15, i.e. by roughly one-sixth (more exactly about one-seventh). That is the discrepancy Brewster reports.

Neither computation appears on the page. Riemann is collecting historical material, probably for his natural-philosophy notes.
errors: Brewster's error, copied faithfully: Oldenburg died in September 1677, not August 1678, and Hooke became secretary in 1677.

Brewster overstates Hooke's role: Hooke did not 'prove' the path would be an eccentric ellipse. He asserted an 'elliptueid' curve, and inside the earth the true path under a linear force is a centred ellipse.

The 1682 Picard anecdote (Newton too agitated to finish the calculation) is regarded by modern historians (e.g. Cajori 1928, Whiteside) as a legend. Picard's measurement was known in England well before 1682.
Brewster says 'calculation of 1665' after earlier placing the episode in 1666. Plague-year chronology is loose in the source.
The 'one-sixth' discrepancy with 60 miles per degree is approximate: the ratio 69.1/60 ≈ 1.15 is closer to one-seventh. Brewster's figure comes from Pemberton/Whiston tradition.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a verbatim reading excerpt from Brewster's 1831 Newton biography with no original mathematics. It only shows Riemann's interest in the history of gravitation theory, which fits his known natural-philosophy notes.

checkable.asserts: With T^2 = k r^3, the centripetal acceleration 4 pi^2 r/T^2 equals 4 pi^2/(k r^2), an inverse-square law (expression simplifies to 0).
Using 60 instead of ~69.1 miles per degree makes the predicted force exceed the observed one by a factor ≈ 1.15 (about 1/6-1/7 greater).
With correct modern data, g/60^2 matches the moon's centripetal acceleration to within about 1% (ratio ≈ 1).

transcription_corrections: Heading: the machine reading 'veröffentlichten[?]' is plausible ('Geschichte der in den Principien veröffentlichten Entdeckungen Newtons'). The hand is cramped and the word is uncertain.
'garden at Cambridge Wools-thorpe': the manuscript does appear to read 'Cambridge Wools-thorpe' (a slip; Brewster has simply 'Woolsthorpe'), so the '[?]' can be dropped.
Before 'he found that the force which retains the moon': the struck-out word reads like 'he found'. The second copy is written as 'found' with an overwritten initial ('ound').
Marginal 'p. 150' is written 'p.150' immediately before 'After'. The struck word before 'return' looks like 'speent'/'speedy' and is cancelled.
'promised to sent to the Society': the manuscript indeed reads 'sent', a slip for Brewster's 'send'.
